name: Mattole-Bear River
confidence_why: One first-hand description, Li 1930 (the published form of Li's 1929 dissertation), checked against the source: stress (Li's 'accent', which 'denotes stress' in Mattole, p. 5 n. 3) is placed relative to the stem, is weak, and a residue of nouns has 'no definite rule'; no tone ('Mattole is not a tonal language', p. 3). Grune 1994 is a secondary summary whose only linguistic reference is Li 1930.

new_statements.quote: 56. Accent: Mattole cannot be said to be a strongly accented language; there is a tendency to accent the stem-syllable, which is usually the last, or the syllable immediately preceding the stem. If the accent falls on the last syllable, it usually consists of a higher pitch if the vowel is short, or a slightly rising intonation if the vowel is long. ... [p. 51] For verbs the accent is either on the syllable preceding the stem or on the stem. The latter occurs particularly when the stem is in the heavy form. ... The accent is, however, shifted to the stem if there is a suffix following it. [p. 5 n. 3] Accent mark in Hupa, Wailaki, and Mattole denotes stress; in Sarcee and Navaho, pitch.

new_statements.relation_note: new: nothing on record (no catalog record, no statement held by the project for matt1238). Compatible with the secondary restatement held held by the project (Grune 1994 p. 2: 'Stress is generally on the last syllable, but may fall on the one but last syllable, especially in third person verb forms and in some nouns'), which paraphrases this passage; Li's own formulation is stem-oriented (stem syllable, usually last, or the pre-stem syllable) rather than purely positional.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Weak, non-contrastive word accent (= stress, per p. 5 n. 3) oriented to the stem: it tends to fall on the stem syllable, which is usually word-final, or else on the syllable immediately before the stem. Nouns: possessed monosyllabic noun stems and deverbal nouns are stem(final)-accented; a few nouns with a vocalic or nasal prefix accent the prefix; some nouns follow no rule. Verbs: accent on the pre-stem syllable or on the stem, the stem especially in its heavy form; any suffix after the stem pulls the accent onto the stem. Final accent is realised as higher pitch on a short vowel or a slight rise on a long vowel; Mattole has no tone marking (accent mark = stress).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing on secondary stress; Li describes a single weak accent per word.
new_statements.exceptions: Prefix-accented nouns (ci-tse' 'my penis', cintsin 'the center of my breast', cintcxix 'my nose', ci-ge' 'my marrow', cila' 'my hand'); nouns for which 'no definite rule can be deduced' (txa-ba' 'hunger', da-tci-x 'sweat house', ba-tco' 'ocean', ba'nin 'enemy'); light-stem verbs with pre-stem accent ('ican 'I eat', 'onge 'you spear at him', dicba' 'I go to war') vs heavy/suffixed stems accented on the stem. (Mattole forms given here without diacritics; see the page scan.)
new_statements.identity_note: Li 1930 describes Mattole proper (fieldwork 1927, Mattole River drainage, Humboldt County, California); Bear River is named only as former territory and no separate Bear River dialect data appear in the pages read. Goddard 1929 (Bear River dialect, already read: silent on stress) covers the other member of matt1238.

sources.note: States flatly that Mattole, unlike most Athabaskan languages, has no tones, with stress generally on the last syllable (sometimes the penult); p. 6 contrasts Navaho's two tones (every syllable tone-bearing) with toneless Mattole. This restates Li 1930 pp. 3-4 ('Mattole is not a tonal language') and sec. 56.
